Introduction
Hello, I’m Kara.

I’ve been making pottery for nearly 20 years, and at the time of
writing this I’ve been a full-time potter for 9 years. That doesn’t
even seem possible, but  it’s true. I’m predominantly a self-taught
potter. I’ve had my work stocked in Fortnum & Mason. I’ve made
plates for a Michelin-starred restaurant. I’ve taught hundreds of
people pottery via workshops both in person and online via my
Pottery Club. And I’m the author of Pottery for Beginners.
A few years ago, I was searching for a good pottery notebook but
couldn’t find one, so I created my own. Here it is. This notebook
began as a way of keeping notes of my own kiln firings. Originally it
was just in digital format, but as time went on, I knew how much
my fellow potters would benefit from this tool and how useful it
would be to make it into a real-life book that you can hold in your
hands. It has evolved to include a ton of information on how to
make your firings more successful, as well as an area to record your
making processes too.
This notebook is a companion tool for all your pottery adventures.
Keeping a pottery notebook doesn’t just help you get excellent,
repeatable results; it’s also a lovely way to look back at your skill
progression. Treat it like an artist’s sketchbook or diary with added
useful data. I hope this will always be your go-to notebook and a
place to keep your notes for reference and posterity.




    TIP FOR ELECTRIC KILN OWNERS
     In this notebook there are 120 pages to record 120 firings. The
    average set of kiln elements lasts 100 firings. It’s a great idea to
     start a new notebook when you get a new kiln or a new set of
    elements. When you’re nearing the end of your notebook  is
   when your elements might be wearing out and need changing.

(Although this depends upon a few different factors, which I
explain here.)

PRO TIPS
• Sketch out designs in clay as well as on paper. This will help you
 figure out if a design will work in 3D as well as in 2D. Gravity
 plays an important role in pottery!
• Keep a prototype of each design you are happy with. This will help
 you to replicate it in the future.

Calculating Shrinkage Rates
Everything you make will shrink approximately 10 to 20 percent on
average from the wet raw clay to final firing. It’s important to know
how much. Most manufacturers list the shrinkage rate of the clay on
their packaging, but you can also calculate it by making a shrinkage
ruler.
Roll out a slab of your clay ¼ inch (0.6 cm) thick. Using a plastic
ruler as a template, cut out two ruler shapes. Mark on them the
inches or centimeters. Then leave them to dry. Pop one ruler in the
glaze firing and one in the bisque. Then measure your fired rulers
and compare them to the original to see the shrinkage rate of your
clay  at  the  different  stages  of making. When recording the
dimensions of your greenware, make sure you record whether
it is freshly thrown, leather hard or bone dry.
Formula
100% - [(Fired Ruler Length / Original Ruler Length) × 100]% =
shrinkage percentage
Example
Original Ruler Length: 30 cm
Fired Ruler Length: 27 cm
27 / 30 = 0.9 × 100 = 90
Shrinkage rate = 100% – 90% = 10%

The longest, dark brown ruler on the far left shows the clay in its raw
state—fresh out of the bag. The ruler next to it shows the clay in its bone
dry or greenware state. The third ruler has been bisque fired. The ruler
on  the  far  right (though not  glazed) has been  fired  to glazeware
temperatures.

Calculating Specific Gravity
Measuring the specific gravity of your glaze is a way of checking
you have the correct  ratio of water to glaze material. This  is
especially relevant for dipping glazes and for those who make their
own glazes from raw materials based on a recipe.
Specific gravity has to do with the “fit” of the glaze. Imagine the
glaze is like clothing that the clay wears. If there is too much glaze
material in the glaze, the clothing may become too tight. Put stress
on the clay (such as pouring in hot water), and the clothing may
tear. This can create faults in your pottery, such as a crack. Too
little glaze material in the glaze and it may become too weak. This
may make  it very powdery before  it’s fired and chip easily. The
color of the glaze may also come out wishy-washy or brown.
Most glazes work best between 1.4 and 1.6, but there are exceptions
to this. Only by testing will you find the correct specific gravity of
your glaze. You can measure specific gravity using a graduated
cylinder and a digital scale. Note: Make sure you  stir the glaze
really well before measuring.
Specific Gravity Formula
Weight in grams of glaze / Volume in ml of the glaze
Example
700 grams / 500 ml = 1.4
Keeping the specific gravity of your glaze consistent at a ratio you
know works well will help you to reproduce good glaze results.
 • If your specific gravity is too high, you need to add water. Do this
  gradually, recalculating the gravity in between.

•  If your  specific gravity  is too low, you can add more glaze
  material or you can allow the glaze to settle overnight and syphon
  off some of the water.

Calculating Cost of Firings
If your kiln controller does not give you information on KW usage or
cost,  here’s a formula  to help you!  You’ll need the following
information:
 • Cost of electricity per kilowatt hour (kWh) – These vary from
  location to location, so make sure to look up your local electricity
   tariff.
 • Kilowatt rating of the kiln – This is normally written on a metal
  panel on the side of the kiln.
 • Program duration in hours.
 • Duty cycle of the kiln – The elements are not on for the entire
  firing cycle. A duty cycle of the kiln  is the amount of time
  electricity  is actually passing through the elements, when the
  relays are turned on. You will hear when the relays turn on and
   off by the clicks. A duty cycle is typically 60%. You would express
  this value as a decimal, e.g., 0.6.
Formula
(Cost of electricity per kilowatt hour) × (kilowatt rating of the kiln)
× (program duration in hours) × (duty cycle of the kiln)
Example
$0.35 × 7.5 × 8 hours × 0.6 = $12.60
   PRO TIP
    Take photos of your pots and put them into a digital folder
     labeled with the corresponding number of your firing and the
     date. It’s a great idea to take a photo of your cones too so you
    can have a visual reference of the heat work without needing to
    keep all your cones.

Firing Glossary
Heat work: Heat work is the combined effect of heat over a period
of time. As potters, we are much more concerned with heat work
versus purely temperature. It takes the accumulation of heat over a
period of time for clay and glaze to absorb the heat work it needs to
become ceramic. A bit like in your home oven, we can either cook
something at a high temperature for a shorter period of time or at a
low temperature for a longer period of time.
Top temperature: This  is the highest temperature the kiln will
reach during your firing.
Schedule: This is the temperature you want your kiln to get to and
how fast you want it to get there. It can be slow, medium or fast on
a manual or gas kiln, or it may be done in ramps (see below for
explanation of ramp) on a digital controller.
Ramp: This refers to how many degrees per hour your kiln will heat
up as programmed into its digital controller (e.g., 212°F [100°C] per
hour).
Soak: This refers to holding the top temperature for a period of time
(normally in 15-minute increments) to help even out the heat work
throughout the kiln. The middle of a kiln tends to be hottest, with
cooler shelves at the bottom. You may want to add a soak to a glaze
firing to even out the temperature, making sure all shelves reach the
same cone. Or pack the kiln more heavily in the middle. This is
especially useful in larger kilns. For example: For my large 117-liter
kiln,  I add a 15-minute soak at 2183°F (1195°C) for my cone 6
firings. This evens out the temperature throughout my kiln before
the firing then climbs to its final temperature of 2232°F (1222°C).

Vitrification (or maturity): Clay and glaze remain porous and
relatively weak until they are fired to their vitrification temperature.
You need your pots to be glazed, fired and vitrified or fired to
maturity in order to hold your coffee. It is important to note the
firing temperature of your clay and glazes when you buy them, as
this will inform the temperature the kiln must be fired to. Your clay
and glaze temperatures must always be within the same  firing
range.





Element wear: Elements generally last between 50 to 150 firings
(average being 100), but this varies depending on things such as the
temperature you fire to and the glazes you use. Hotter firings wear
elements quicker. A potter using cone 10 porcelain may need to
change their elements sooner than a potter using cone 6 stoneware.
As the elements in a kiln age, your firings will likely take longer,
and it will take more energy to pass a current through the element.
Eventually, they might not even be able to reach temperature at all!
The longer your firings take and the longer elements spend at a
higher temperature, the more they wear. Certain materials in glaze

recipes will also wear your elements more than others. Keeping
peepholes open until 1112°F (600°C) can help elements last longer
as this allows corrosive vapors to escape. Having a downdraft vent
will help pull vapors out of the kiln and away from elements,
making them last longer.
Using cones and keeping accurate notes of how long your firings are
taking will help you predict when you need to change your elements
—which is much better than getting caught out a week before your
next craft market! Other parts of a kiln can wear out too such as the
thermocouple and relays. Keeping a record of how many firings
your kiln has done will help you maintain your kiln’s health and
ensure it keeps firing consistently.

What Are Cones?

Cones are made of ceramic material just like your clay and glazes.
They are designed to melt and bend at very specific temperatures
according to how much heat work they have been exposed to during
a firing.
In most modern digital kilns, temperature is measured by the kiln’s
thermocouple  at a  single spot  in the  kiln and  is displayed  in
Fahrenheit or Celsius on your kiln’s digital controller.
As we know, heat work takes things a step further and  is the
accumulative  effect that temperature has over a period  of  time.
Pyrometric cones are the only real way of reading the heat
work your pottery has absorbed. They may sound technical, but
they are a useful little tool for all potters.
Some clays and glazes have a wide firing range, while others need
much more accuracy to get the desired results. So many issues we
encounter as potters have to do with what goes on inside our kiln
(e.g., if your glazes ran during a firing, this could mean the glaze
was applied too thickly or your kiln overfired). Cones help us
understand if we have underfired, overfired or reached our desired
heat work. If the cones look good, we can rule out the firing as an
issue. By using cones in all our glaze firings, accurately recording
our processes and results, we can identify issues and replicate good
results next time.

Small cone on the left compared to a large standard cone in the middle
and a self-supporting cone on the right.





A cone pack consisting of cone 4, cone 5 and cone 6.
Types of Cones
Cones range from cone 022 very low temperature to cone 14 very
high temperature. See cone charts here for equivalent temperatures.

Small Cones and Bar Cones: These are used in a kiln sitter in a
manual kiln. These bend and drop the lever to shut off the kiln
when    it  has  reached  temperature.  They  cannot  be  used
interchangeably with standard or self-supporting cones. Note: I won’t be
referring to these throughout this book as they bend differently than
standard or self-supporting cones. If you use a manual kiln, I still
recommend using standard or self-supporting cones to record the
heat work in your firings.
Standard Cones: These are referred to as witness cones, as they are
literally  “witnessing  the  firing.” These can be  stood  in  small
sausages of clay to create a cone pack. (See How to Use Cones to
learn how to make a cone pack.)

Three cone 7 self-supporting cones.
Self-Supporting Cones: These are also referred to as witness cones,
but they have a small additional triangle at the base, which means
they stand up on their own and do not need clay sausages. They are
a little more expensive, but you can always be sure they are at the
correct angle, and they don’t need to be placed into clay.
I  will be  referring  to both standard and  self-supporting cones
interchangeably throughout this notebook.
How to Use Cones

Always use the cones that match the temperature of the glazes and
clay you are using.
Be careful: Cone 06 and cone 6 are very different!
 • A cone 6 will bend at around 2232°F (1222°C) depending upon the
  speed of the firing. This is a mid-fire or low stoneware.
 • Cone 06 will bend at around 1830°F (999°C), so it is for low-fire or
  earthenware.
To use cones, you normally use three. This is called a “cone pack.”
For a cone 6 firing you would use cone 5, cone 6 and cone 7.





The above image is a 6 cone pack.
 • The Guide Cone (cone 5) is the one to the left.
 • The Target Cone (cone 6) is the middle cone—the heat work or
  cone you are aiming for.
 • The Guard Cone (cone 7) is the one to the right.
Making a Cone Pack
You can put standard large cones into a little sausage of soft clay
(no bigger than the thickness of a pencil). Gently push the cone all
the way through the clay until the base is touching the surface of
the table. This ensures they are sitting at the correct angle, which is

determined by the slope of the base. You can squash the clay back
around the base to keep them in place if need be.
Poke the clay with a needle tool (as shown in the image above) to
ensure  any  water  quickly  escapes  in  the  firing  and  avoids
explosions. You can wait until the clay is bone dry before putting it
in the  kiln.  I normally make a whole bunch of cone packs in
advance so they are ready and dry when I need them.
If you are using specifically made cone holders, like the one on here,
make sure the falling face always goes next to the dot. (If you stand
a cone on a table, the falling face is the direction the cone falls.)
   NOTE
      If you try to stand a standard large cone up on its own, it will
      fall over. This is due to the specific angle of the base which,
    with the help of gravity, ensures the cone bends correctly.
    Ensuring the cones are at the correct angle is important. If you
    stand a cone on a table the falling face is the direction the cone
      falls.





The cone pack on the left is correct; note the slight lean to the left. The
cone pack on the right is incorrect; note they are pointing straight up and
won’t bend properly in the firing.

Cone Placement
With gas and wood firings, potters put cone packs near the vents or
peepholes so they can be observed during the firing. This must be
done wearing welding goggles or there is a risk to the eyesight. In
my experience with electric kilns, and certainly those new to firing
their own kilns,  it  is very awkward to get cones in the correct
position and difficult to see them when the kiln is white hot. It’s
best to look at cones retrospectively—that is after the firing.
We need to put the cones far enough away from our work so when
they bend they don’t stick to it. The middle of a kiln shelf is best
and is the most accurate representation of heat work. For larger
kilns, it’s best to put a cone pack on the bottom, middle and top
shelf. For smaller kilns, you shouldn’t get a lot of difference in heat
work between shelves, so one cone pack on the middle shelf will
normally suffice.
   NOTE
    Be careful when handling cones as they are fragile and can
    break easily. Hold the ends and twist them apart. Or hold one
    on the end, flush to the edge of a table and push down on the
     other. See the image below for reference.

Good to know:
 • Cones lose their color after they’ve been fired and turn white. This
   is so that even if the cones haven’t bent, you know they’ve been
  used.
 • You can only use cones once.
 • Specifically made cone holders, like the one on here, are single
  use. As a reminder, the falling face always goes next to the dot.

How to Read Cones (Have You
Had a Successful Firing?)
You know you have the perfect heat work when the guide cone
(left) melts  first and  likely melts completely. The  target cone
(middle) will bend over next in an elegant arc. The guard cone
(right) will remain straight or only start to bend slightly.





This firing has reached a perfect cone 6.





Contrary to popular belief, the tip does not have to touch the kiln shelf.
Example of Overfiring
Image 1 shows that the firing was too hot. These cones absorbed too
much heat work. The glazes and clay in this kiln load may show

signs of overfiring (e.g., running, blistering, bloating, etc.).
How to fix:  I’ll need to reduce the temperature of the kiln next
time, speed up the firing, remove the soak or a combination of all
three.





Overfiring: All the cones, including the guard cone, have melted and bent
all the way over.
Example of Underfiring
Image 2 shows the work on  this  shelf  didn’t  quite reach the
temperature I wanted. This tells me my pottery and cones did not
absorb enough heat work to vitrify cone 6 clay and glazes.
How to fix: I’ll need to increase the top temperature of my firing
schedule, slow down the firing or add a soak onto the end of my
firing next time.
The key is in the tip of the cone. If the tip is still angled up, it hasn’t
quite reached the temperature range required. Once the  tip  is
pointing down, the melt of the cone is quite rapid.

Underfiring: Note that the middle cone, cone 6 which is the target cone,
has only bent a little bit. This was more like a cone 5.5 firing.
PRO TIP
The difference between the bend in these two cones represents only
about 35 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius)!





Note the tip is touching the table.

Note the tip is pointing down but hasn’t quite touched the table. As long
as your tip is angled down you are within the target cone tolerance.
You will need to put cones in  all glaze  firings to ensure your
adjustments have had the desired effect and maintain consistency.
Don’t forget to record what you did and your results straight away
in your notebook!
   GOOD TO KNOW
    You don’t need to put cones in all your bisque firings. Our goal
      is not to vitrify our pottery during bisque firings, so it’s not as
     critical    to   ensure  we   have   reached   a    specific
    temperature/amount of heat work.





Variables that can affect heat work:
 • The peak temperature the kiln reached.
 • The period of time the work is in the kiln.
 • The amount of work in the firing. Tightly packed kilns take longer
  to heat up so the time variable needs to increase, but the top
  temperature will need to be adjusted lower to reach the required
  heat work value.
 • How the shelves are placed. Ensuring shelves are well distributed
  throughout the kiln will help it to heat evenly.

• Some kilns tend to be hotter in the middle. Stacking the middle of
  the kiln more densely with work will help to even out the heat
  work.
Glaze only starts to melt in the final 212°F (100°C) of a firing. Note
the Heating Rate on the cone chart here. This refers to the ramp
used ONLY during the final 212°F (100°C) of the firing.
Slower firings can give more interesting glaze results as it has given
the glazes more time to “mature” (when all the ingredients in the
glaze melt and mingle together). Remember a slower firing will use
more energy.
To get the benefit of a slow firing while also using less energy, it’s
possible to use a relatively fast-firing schedule and then slow the
ramp in the final 212°F (100°C). Alternatively, you could add a soak
period onto the end of your firing. A 15- to 20-minute hold  is
roughly equal to one cone’s worth of heat. You may need to lower
the top temperature to compensate for the additional time, but not
always.
To recap:
 • Putting cones in every glaze firing will help you best understand
  how your kiln is firing.
 • Always refer to the cone chart here to make sure you are using the
  correct cones for your glazes.
 • Cones will always bend in a consistent way in reaction to the heat
  and time they are exposed to in the kiln. From batch to batch they
  are carefully tested by the manufacturer for accuracy.
 • Commercial glazes and clays will always have the cone or firing
  temperature displayed on the packaging.
A quick note about glaze and food safety:

One major way (but not the only way) to ensure pottery is safe to
use with food is to make sure the clay and glazes you use become
fully matured (or cooked) during the firing. This means colorant
oxides become chemically bound into the glaze and are unlikely to
leach out. Keeping accurate notes and using cones in your firings to
ensure you reached the desired heat work are two due diligences
that potters can employ.
Other ways include but are not exclusive to:
 • Only use commercial glazes labeled as lead free and food or
  dinnerware safe.
 • Do not use glaze with lots of texture for surfaces which come in
  contact with food.
 •  If you make your own glazes,  it’s best to steer clear of toxic
  ingredients such as lead, cadmium, barium and lithium.
 • Use color oxides in low percentages (<3%).

Kiln Schedules
There are no one-size-fits-all kiln schedules. The heat work achieved
in your firing relies on many variables. You will need to test some
schedules out to determine the correct firing for your work.





It is to be expected to need to test a new kiln or any new glazes to find
the best schedule for your desired result.
Most firings in an electric kiln (except for luster and decal) take
between 8 to 12 hours and then at least an additional 24 hours to
cool down depending on the size of the kiln. Small kilns tend to cool
faster.
For safety reasons, it is always best to wait until it has cooled to
room temperature before unloading.
New kilns come with a manual and recommended firing schedules.
If you bought your kiln secondhand or don’t have the manual, here
are  some  suggested  general  schedules  for  kilns  with  digital
controllers. These should be used as a starting point as all kilns fire
slightly differently. Even kilns of the same brand and of a similar
size can vary. You may need to adjust these schedules depending on

the clay and glaze you are using and your desired results. For
example, my small 45-liter kiln is so well insulated, it achieves a
cone 6 firing with a top temperature of 2183°F (1195°C).
   NOTE
   A slower firing schedule with a lower top temperature can have
     similar  heat  work  as  a  fast  schedule  at  a  higher  top
    temperature. Which works best for your work depends on the
    type of kiln you use, the clay, glazes, how the kiln is packed
    and the aesthetic you are looking for.





Fast firing

For example, both of these pots were fired in my kiln in two
separate   firings  on   different  schedules  with   different  top

temperatures and ramps. They are the same glaze and the same

Kiln Schedule Examples
Ghost Firing
This is a firing for a new kiln or a new set of elements. This includes
furniture—shelves and stilts—but without any pottery. This helps
oxidize the elements and protect them from fumes and water vapor
damage during  future  firings. Note:  Please  refer  to your  kiln
manufacturer’s manual in the first instance as recommended ghost
firings can vary by brand.

• Ramp 1: 176°F (80°C) per hour to 1112°F (600°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1922°F (1050°C)
   • 1½-hour soak
   • Vents open throughout
Bisque
For bisque firings, you want to take it slow as there may be residual
moisture left in the clay. With the bisque firing we do not need to
vitrify the clay, but only make it less brittle so it is easier to handle
while glazing. Normally, potters will bisque to between 1652 and
1940°F (900 and 1060°C).
   • Ramp 1: 176°F (80°C) per hour to 1112°F (600°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1922°F (1050°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout
Earthenware Glaze Firing
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2102°F (1150°C)
   • No soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)
Fast Stoneware Glaze Firing—Cone 6
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2228°F (1220°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)

Slow Stoneware Glaze Firing—Cone 8
   • Ramp 1: 212°F (100°C) per hour to 572°F (300°C)
   • Ramp 2: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 2050°F (1121°C)
   • Ramp 3: 140°F (60°C) per hour to 2246°F (1230°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Close vents at 1112°F (600°C)
Slow Cool Schedule for Crystalline Glazes
Add this ramp to the end of either a Fast or Slow Stoneware Glaze
Firing.
   • Drop: 302°F (150°C) per hour to 1940°F (1060°C)
   • Hold: 1.5 hours
   • Cool naturally
Gold Luster Firing—Cone 018
Always refer to luster manufacturer instructions.
   • Ramp 1: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 1274–1292°F (690–700°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout
Over Glaze Decals Firing—Cones 011–012
Always refer to decal manufacturer instructions.
   • Ramp 1: 338°F (170°C) per hour to 788°F (420°C)
   • Ramp 2: 392°F (200°C) per hour to 1616°F (880°C)
   • 15-minute soak
   • Vents open throughout

Pottery, Efficiency and the Environment
Pottery has an impact on the planet. Keeping accurate notes using
this notebook for all your firings ensures your work will be more
successful. Fewer dud pots means happier potters but also fewer
refires and less waste. Here are some tips to maximize our efficiency
and minimize our environmental impact.
   • When buying a kiln, choose one with the thickest insulation; it
    will be more energy efficient.
   • Firing a full kiln is more energy efficient than firing a half-empty
     kiln. Always fire your kilns full. Tumble stack your bisque. As
    the pottery is unglazed, work can touch and be stacked together
    in the kiln. Make sure you leave a little wiggle room so pieces
    don’t crack each other. Glazed work cannot touch each other, or
      it will stick together!
   • Ensure your work is fully dried before putting it in your kiln.
    This includes after glazing. I always wait 24 hours after glazing
    before loading my kiln.
   • Excess moisture wears your elements quicker and as a result
    they use more energy (not to mention may cause explosions).
   • Fast glaze firings are more energy efficient. When it comes to
    kiln schedules,  it’s a balancing act of using the most energy-
    efficient firing schedule possible while still getting your desired
     results.  There  are  critical  points  of  the  firing where  it’s
    important to go slow, e.g., at the beginning and at the end. Start
    slow, speed it up and slow down again at the end.
   • Your  pots could be around  for  the next 1,000  years! Be
    discerning. Bad work equals landfill. Not every pot needs to be
     fired. Only chose your best work to  fire. Reclaim the  rest.
   Encourage your students to do the same.

• Clay and glazes are mined. Their production has an impact on
  the planet. Ask your pottery supplier where your clay and glaze
  materials come from. Ask  if oxides are responsibly sourced.
  Choose clay sourced from within your country, if possible.
• Use a “three bucket glaze reclaim system.” Rinse all your glazing
  tools in one bucket, then dip a second time in the next bucket. A
  dip in the third bucket should come out clean. Once the first
  bucket  is full of glaze material, use this as a mystery glaze.
  Alternatively, evaporate all the water, fire it in a sacrificial pot
 and throw it away.
• Ensure your local energy is from 100% renewables. This is not
  the same as “backed by” 100% renewable energy.
• Vacuum your kiln every few firings. Dust and debris which
  inevitably build up over time will make the elements work
  harder.
